note: Prices the one-line capture change: `queue max-size-buffers=1 leaky=downstream` now sits ahead of videoconvert/videoscale in minimal/capture_wayland.py instead of at the end of the chain. The argv is r2026-11-08-1080p-window-b's, character for character, so the pair is an A/B and nothing else moved. What that run measured, and what this one has to beat: the chain used **8.52 s of CPU across a 9.50 s window - 90% of one core - while presenting 120 frames**, with a core busy while the worker wanted the CPU for its own 21.71 ms frame; the frame time was **median 36.2 ms / 27.7 fps** at 1080p against 46.6 ms for the 1440p live baseline. The prediction is docs/M0-FINDINGS.md's: `capture cpu:` falls while the frame time does not rise. Read the `capture cpu:` line first, then the median. Two possible outcomes, both useful: the CPU falls and the frame time holds or improves (the change is kept), or the CPU barely moves (frame-dropping was never where the 8.52 s went, and the port's `fullWidth != workWidth` route - which removes the resize outright - is the only half of this residual left). One caveat that must be carried: part of that 9.50 s window was the worker's JIT warm-up with nothing draining the pipe, so some of the 8.52 s is warm-up rather than discarded-frame work; the share is exactly what changes here. The caps are unchanged, so the picture must not move - the before/after PNG hashes are that check, and a changed hash means the queue move altered the frames, which would be a defect rather than a trade.
